summary: In Greek mythology, Phocus was a prince of Aegina, the son of Aeacus and the Nereid Psamathe. His name (Ancient Greek: Φῶκος) means "seal," a reference to the form Psamathe took when Aeacus assaulted her. Favored by his father over his half-brothers Peleus and Telamon, the gifted athlete Phocus was killed by them out of jealousy, and the brothers were exiled from Aegina as a result. He is also remembered as a possible eponym of the region of Phocis.

etymology: His name, Ancient Greek Φῶκος (Phōkos), means "seal." It refers to the circumstances of his conception: his mother, the Nereid Psamathe, transformed herself into a seal when she was ambushed by Aeacus, and Phocus was conceived in that form.

sections.heading: Birth and family
paragraphs: Phocus was a prince of Aegina and the son of Aeacus and Psamathe. His mother Psamathe, the Nereid goddess of sand beaches, transformed herself into a seal when she was ambushed by Aeacus, and was raped as a seal; conceived in the rape, Phocus' name means "seal." According to Pindar, Psamathe gave birth to Phocus on the seashore.
By Asteria or Asterodia, Phocus had twin sons, Crisus and Panopeus.

sections.heading: Death and the exile of his half-brothers
paragraphs: Aeacus favored Phocus over Peleus and Telamon, his two sons with Endeïs. The Bibliotheca characterizes Phocus as a strong athlete, whose athletic ability caused his half-brothers to grow jealous. Their jealousy drove them to murder him during sport practice; Telamon, the stronger half-brother, threw a discus at Phocus' head, killing him.

The brothers hid the corpse in a thicket, but Aeacus discovered the body and punished Peleus and Telamon by exiling them from Aegina. Telamon was sent to Salamis, where he became king after Cychreus, the reigning king, died without an heir, while Peleus went to Phthia, where he was purified by the Phthian king Eurythion.
John Tzetzes relates that Psamathe sent a wolf to avenge her son's death, but when the wolf began to devour Peleus' kine, Thetis changed it into stone.

sections.heading: Variant accounts of his death
paragraphs: The tradition varies with regard to the nature of Phocus' death. Other versions include: Telamon threw a quoit at his head; Telamon killed him with a spear while hunting; Peleus killed him with a stone during a contest in the pentathlon to please Endeïs, as Phocus was her husband's son by a different woman; some authors mention only that Peleus and Telamon killed Phocus out of envy, without details; and other sources say that, whichever brother was responsible, it was an accident.

sections.heading: Eponym of Phocis and cult at Aegina
paragraphs: According to Pausanias, Phocus visited the region that was later called Phocis shortly before his death, with the intent of settling there and gaining rule over the local inhabitants. During his stay there he became friends with Iaseus; Pausanias describes a painting of Phocus giving his seal ring to Iaseus as a sign of friendship, noting that Phocus is portrayed as a youth while Iaseus looks older and has a beard. Elsewhere, Pausanias mentions that Phocus' sons Crisus and Panopaeus emigrated to Phocis.
The tomb of Phocus was shown at Aegina beside the shrine of Aeacus.
